Introduction

The first and most compelling reason for a Christian theocracy is the moral vacuum left by secular governance. Without a divine standard, society inevitably drifts toward relativism—the dangerous notion that truth is subjective and determined by those in power. When morality is not anchored in Scripture, it becomes whatever those in power decree—today’s truth is tomorrow’s heresy.

Christianity, by contrast, provides an unchanging moral framework. The Ten Commandments do not evolve with cultural trends; they stand as eternal guideposts for human flourishing. A theocracy rooted in biblical law would criminalize the slaughter of the innocent, uphold the sanctity of marriage between one man and one woman, and punish blasphemy and idolatry—just as ancient Israel and early Christian societies did. Laws would be based not on partisan interests but on the common good, as defined by Scripture.

A Christian theocracy would end this chaos by establishing a single moral vision—one that unites rather than divides, that calls all people to repentance and reconciliation rather than endless conflict. Far from imposing oppression, such a system would lift people out of the muck of identity politics and restore the dignity of every individual as a creation in God’s image.

Critics of theocracy often equate it with tyranny, picturing priests in robes wielding the sword of the state. Charlemagne, Saint Louis of France, and Alfred the Great were not just warriors—they were patrons of learning, protectors of the poor, and reformers of justice. A Christian theocracy would prioritize the sick, the orphan, the widow, and the stranger—not out of political calculation, but out of worship for the God who commanded, “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Mark 12:31).

A Nation Under God: The Case for an Explicitly Christian American Republic

Introduction

America stands at a crossroads. For two and a half centuries, this nation has drifted between the Christian convictions that shaped its founding and the secular pluralism that now dominates its institutions. The time has come to resolve this tension decisively—not through compromise, but through a forthright return to the theological foundation upon which Western civilization, and America in particular, was built. The Historical Argument

The claim that America was founded as a secular nation is a revisionist myth. The Mayflower Compact of 1620 begins, "In the name of God, Amen," and declares its purpose as undertaken "for the Glory of God, and advancement of the Christian Faith." Eleven of the thirteen original colonies had established churches or explicit religious tests for office. The Massachusetts Constitution, drafted by John Adams in 1780, declared that "the happiness of a people and the good order and preservation of civil government essentially depend on piety, religion, and morality."

Even the Declaration of Independence appeals four times to divine authority: to "Nature's God," to "the Creator," to "the Supreme Judge of the world," and to "divine Providence." These were not deistic flourishes but reflections of a worldview in which rights, law, and legitimacy flowed from God. John Jay, the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, wrote that "Providence has given to our people the choice of their rulers, and it is the duty, as well as the privilege and interest of our Christian nation to select and prefer Christians for their rulers."

The First Amendment's prohibition on a national establishment was meant to prevent federal interference with state establishments, not to secularize the public square. To recover America's foundation is not innovation—it is restoration.

The Philosophical Argument

All law is the imposition of someone's moral vision. The secular pretense of neutrality is itself a theological claim—a claim that God is either absent or irrelevant to public life. Every legal code answers questions that are ultimately religious: What is a human being? What is justice? What do we owe one another? Why should the strong restrain themselves toward the weak?

Secular liberalism borrows its core commitments—human dignity, equality before the law, the restraint of power, care for the vulnerable—from the Christian tradition it now disavows. The philosopher Jürgen Habermas, himself a secularist, acknowledged that "egalitarian universalism, from which sprang the ideas of freedom and a social solidarity... is the direct legacy of the Judaic ethic of justice and the Christian ethic of love. To this day, there is no alternative to it."

A society that cuts itself off from the source of its moral vocabulary will eventually lose the vocabulary itself. The cultural fragmentation, epidemic loneliness, and declining social trust of contemporary America are symptoms of this severance. Explicit Christian governance would reconnect public life to its moral roots.

The Practical Argument

Christian principles produce concrete civic goods. The biblical vision of imago Dei—that every human bears the image of God—provides a firmer foundation for human rights than any secular alternative, which must ultimately ground rights in utility, consensus, or power. The prophetic tradition's demands for justice toward the poor, the widow, and the stranger shaped Western welfare, abolitionism, and civil rights. The Christian doctrine of human fallenness produced the institutional checks and balances that restrain tyranny.

A polity that openly acknowledges these sources can cultivate them. Civic education could teach the virtues—faith, hope, love, prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance—that sustain self-government. Laws concerning marriage, the family, the Sabbath, honest commerce, and the protection of unborn life could reflect the accumulated moral wisdom of two thousand years of Christian reflection rather than the shifting preferences of secular elites.

What of religious minorities? A Christian commonwealth need not—and, on Christian principles, must not—coerce belief. Christianity teaches that faith unforced is the only faith worth having. Is this not theocracy? In the strict sense of clerical rule, no. What is proposed is a Christian republic: elected government operating under explicit acknowledgment that its authority derives from God and that its laws must conform to His moral law. This is closer to the vision of the American Founders than to Geneva under Calvin or Iran under the ayatollahs.

Christian Theocracy in the United States: Arguments, Tensions, and Constitutional Limits

The proposal that the United States should become an explicitly Christian nation governed by Christian theological principles raises fundamental questions about political authority, religious liberty, citizenship, and the purpose of democratic government. Advocates of such a system often argue that public life cannot be morally neutral: every legal system reflects some underlying view of human dignity, justice, family, responsibility, and the common good. The debate therefore requires distinguishing between the legitimate influence of religious moral reasoning in public life and the establishment of a state empowered to enforce one religious doctrine.

Supporters of Christian governance often begin with the observation that American political culture has been shaped by Christian ideas. Many early American leaders used religious language, public institutions historically reflected Protestant norms, and movements such as abolitionism, civil rights activism, prison reform, and charitable work were frequently energized by Christian conviction. Concepts including the equal worth of persons, duties toward the poor, the moral limits of power, and the accountability of rulers to a higher standard have often been expressed in Christian terms.

Proponents may also argue that modern political systems are never genuinely value-neutral. Laws regarding marriage, education, abortion, poverty, speech, sexuality, criminal punishment, and the family inevitably make moral judgments. If the state already reflects moral beliefs, they ask, why should Christian convictions be excluded from public policy simply because they are religious? In this view, believers should be free to advocate laws shaped by their faith just as secular citizens advocate laws shaped by philosophical, ideological, or ethical commitments.

That argument has real force in a democracy. Religious citizens do not lose their civic voice when they enter public life. They may vote, organize, speak, campaign, hold office, and offer moral arguments rooted in scripture and tradition. American pluralism does not require believers to conceal their faith; it requires that they participate without using state power to deny equal citizenship to those who do not share it.

The difficulty arises when religious influence becomes religious establishment. A theocracy does not simply permit Christian perspectives in democratic debate. It grants official governing authority to Christian doctrine, institutions, or religious leaders. Laws become binding not because citizens have accepted them through constitutional processes and public reasoning, but because a particular interpretation of divine will is treated as politically supreme. This changes the relationship between citizen and state in a profound way.

The United States Constitution was designed to prevent precisely that concentration of religious and governmental power. The First Amendment prohibits Congress from making laws “respecting an establishment of religion” while protecting the “free exercise” of religion. These principles were not intended to expel religion from society. Rather, they sought to ensure that government could not compel religious conformity or elevate one faith above others. The Constitution’s prohibition on religious tests for public office reinforces the same principle: political membership is not conditional on adherence to a preferred theology.

An official Christian state would immediately raise difficult questions. Which Christianity would govern? Catholic, Baptist, Pentecostal, Lutheran, Orthodox, Reformed, Mormon, Anglican, or another tradition? Christians differ deeply on baptism, sacraments, church authority, divorce, war, gender roles, immigration, wealth, punishment, and the relationship between church and state. History suggests that this danger is not theoretical. Whenever governments have claimed religious authority, dissenters have often faced discrimination, censorship, legal punishment, exclusion from public office, or violence. Such systems have harmed Jews, Muslims, atheists, religious minorities, and Christians outside the favored denomination. The coercive machinery of the state—courts, police, prisons, taxation, licensing, military power—can transform religious disagreement into a matter of political loyalty.

A Christian critique of theocracy may also rest on theological grounds. Many Christians believe faith must be freely chosen rather than imposed. Religious conversion obtained through legal pressure, social punishment, or state coercion is not genuine spiritual conviction. When Christianity becomes the instrument of state power, the church may gain privilege but lose moral independence. It may become reluctant to criticize unjust rulers who claim to defend the faith.

Christian ethics call for mercy, forgiveness, humility, love of enemies, care for the poor, and moral self-examination. Governments, by contrast, must administer laws among people who disagree profoundly about religious truth. A state that claims divine authority may become especially resistant to correction, because political opposition can be portrayed not simply as disagreement but as rebellion against God.

The strongest democratic alternative is neither secular hostility toward religion nor religious domination of the state. It is a constitutional order in which faith can shape citizens and public debate while government remains accountable to all citizens equally. The question is whether the government should wield Christianity as an official source of coercive authority. A society cannot govern without some conception of what is good, true, and worth protecting. Law is always downstream of moral vision. The only real question is whether a nation’s moral orthodoxy will be explicit, accountable, and ennobling—or implicit, fragmented, and subject to the whims of fashion and power. Establishing the United States as an explicitly Christian commonwealth—anchoring governance and law in Christian theological principles while protecting civil liberties—offers a coherent, humane, and time-tested framework for social order, human dignity, and flourishing. Properly understood, this is not a call for clerical rule or coerced conversion, but for a constitutional settlement that acknowledges the moral sources from which our most cherished rights historically flowed and makes them transparent, normative, and durable.

At the heart of the Christian vision is the conviction that every human being bears the image of God. From that single premise flow the central commitments that Americans already claim to prize: inherent dignity, equality before the law, protection of the weak, and limits on the power of the state to instrumentalize persons. The modern language of human rights did not spring from a moral vacuum; it is the legacy of a Christian inheritance that insisted kings and commoners alike stand under a transcendent moral order. By rooting the American regime explicitly in that inheritance, we reinforce the foundation beneath rights we increasingly treat as preferences—thereby making those rights more resilient when cultural winds shift.

Christianity also offers a thick vision of virtue and society—one that law can channel without micromanaging souls. Consider a few pillars. First, the sanctity of life, which safeguards the unborn, the disabled, and the aged from being treated as burdens rather than persons. Second, the primacy of family, understood as the first school of love and the most effective unit for the formation of character; a legal order can support marriage, parenthood, and intergenerational responsibility through tax structures, labor law, and education policy. Third, stewardship, which both disciplines markets against exploitation and honors enterprise, property, and creativity as gifts to be used for the common good. Fourth, justice tempered by mercy: a system that prizes proportionality, due process, rehabilitation, and the possibility of redemption. These are not sectarian eccentricities. They are the very conditions of a humane civilization.

An explicitly Christian polity also clarifies the purpose and limits of government. Christian political thought has long emphasized subsidiarity: responsibilities should rest at the lowest competent level, close to the people who know and love those affected. That principle decentralizes power, empowers families, churches, and civic associations, and guards against bureaucratic overreach. Paired with sphere sovereignty—the conviction that different social institutions (family, church, business, state) have distinct roles—subsidiarity prevents the state from swallowing civil society or privatizing the public good. The result is not theocracy in the caricatured sense, but a constitutional ecosystem that keeps power bounded by purpose, protecting the independence and vitality of non-state communities that actually form people in virtue.

Critics will invoke pluralism and conscience, as well they should. A Christian commonwealth does not compel belief; it acknowledges that faith cannot be coerced and that conscience must be respected. Toleration for non-Christian citizens and religious minorities is not a concession but a command under Christian ethics. The polity can set a Christian moral horizon for law—defining marriage, honoring Sabbath rhythms in public life, setting boundaries around the commodification of bodies, protecting life at its most vulnerable—while guaranteeing freedom of worship, freedom of speech, and freedom of association for all. Historical abuses arose where rulers confused zeal with coercion or entangled church hierarchy with civil administration. A wise American model would codify strict safeguards: no forced religious observance, no religious tests for private employment, due process protections for dissenters, and a clear line between ecclesial governance and civil office. The public square can honor Christian truth without collapsing church into state or state into church.

Nor does explicit Christian grounding undermine scientific progress, artistic freedom, or economic vitality. On the contrary, Christian confidence in a rational, ordered creation and a moral lawgiver historically catalyzed scientific inquiry and the rule of law. A Christian moral economy—insisting on honest weights, fair contracts, care for workers, and protection of the poor—builds durable trust, which is the invisible capital of markets. Cultural creativity thrives where meaning is robust; art and scholarship wither under both nihilism and propaganda. The Christian vision nourishes a culture that takes truth, beauty, and goodness seriously enough to pursue them.

Practically, what might this look like? Constitutionally, an amendment could acknowledge the nation’s Christian character and articulate principles—imago Dei, sanctity of life, marriage and family as foundational institutions, religious liberty as a matter of both truth and peace, and the limits of state power under God. Statutory law could reflect those principles in humane, non-coercive ways: robust support for families and children; incentives for adoption and community-based care; protections for conscience in medicine and education; safeguards against predatory industries that target addiction or degrade the body; rhythms of rest that restore civil life and make room for worship and family; strong protections for the poor, the elderly, and the disabled; rehabilitation-focused criminal justice that pairs accountability with pathways to restoration. Education policy could ensure that parents have meaningful choice and that students encounter the civilizational sources—including Christian scripture and tradition—that shaped the nation’s moral grammar. None of this forbids disagreement. It instead provides the shared moral frame within which disagreements can be reasoned, not merely shouted.

Objections will persist. Some will argue that explicit Christian commitment marginalizes non-Christians. But there is a difference between public orthodoxy and private compulsion. Every regime has an orthodoxy: today’s largely secular, therapeutic one is enforced through law, media, and bureaucracy while pretending to neutrality. The candor of a Christian commonwealth makes its commitments discussable and challengeable; the pretense of neutrality makes secular commitments unaccountable. Others will cite history’s failures. We should. Then we should also note the corrective resources in Christianity itself—repentance, reform, and the prophetic critique of power—and embed structural safeguards so that the state serves genuine justice rather than baptizing injustice.

All societies form souls. The only question is whether they admit it and whether their formation aims at the good. The United States has reached a point where its tacit moral order is both powerful and thin—a set of sentiments about autonomy and harm that cannot bear the weight of human life together. Regrounding American law and governance in explicitly Christian principles would not end debate; it would ennoble it. It would not erase diversity; it would bind it to a shared account of human dignity. And it would place our public life under a moral horizon sturdy enough to protect the vulnerable, humble enough to restrain power, and hopeful enough to inspire sacrifice for the common good. Far from a retreat into the past, this is a recovery of the deep roots that once nourished our freedoms—and could again.

One Nation Under God: The Case for Christian Governance in America

A Persuasive Essay

Introduction

The American experiment, for all its remarkable achievements, finds itself in a period of profound moral disorientation. Rising rates of despair, institutional distrust, family dissolution, and cultural fragmentation suggest that something foundational has gone wrong—not merely at the level of policy, but at the level of first principles. This essay contends that the remedy lies not in further secularization but in its reversal: the United States should reconstitute itself as an explicitly Christian commonwealth, with its laws, institutions, and public life ordered according to Christian theological principles. This is not a call for mere cultural Christianity or civic religion, but for a substantive reorientation of governance toward transcendent truth.

This argument will be unfamiliar and uncomfortable to modern ears trained in the assumptions of liberal secularism. But intellectual discomfort is not refutation. The case for Christian governance rests on coherent philosophical grounds, credible historical precedent, a frank assessment of secularism's failures, and a vision of human flourishing that the contemporary order has proven unable to sustain.

I. The Philosophical Foundation: Government Requires Moral Authority Beyond Itself

Every political order rests on pre-political commitments—assumptions about human nature, moral truth, the purpose of community, and the source of authority. The critical question is never whether a state will be founded on metaphysical premises, but which metaphysical premises will prevail.

Liberal secularism claims neutrality, but this claim dissolves under scrutiny. The secular state does not abstain from moral judgment; it makes moral judgments constantly—about rights, about equality, about justice, about the limits of freedom. It simply refuses to name or ground these judgments in any coherent philosophical framework. The result is a political order that borrows extensively from the Christian moral inheritance—the dignity of the individual, the obligation to the poor, the wrongness of cruelty—while systematically severing these commitments from the theological roots that gave them life and coherence.

This is not philosophically sustainable. As thinkers from Alasdair MacIntyre to Charles Taylor have demonstrated, moral concepts that are extracted from their originating frameworks do not remain stable. They become confused, contested, and eventually hollow. When a civilization insists on Christian-derived moral conclusions while repudiating Christian premises, it lives on borrowed capital, and that capital is rapidly being spent.

Christian theocratic governance addresses this problem directly. It provides what secular liberalism cannot: a coherent account of why human beings possess dignity (they are created in the image of God), why justice matters (God is just and commands justice), why the powerful owe obligations to the weak (Christ identifies with the least of these), and why law has moral authority (it participates in or reflects the divine law). These are not arbitrary assertions but conclusions drawn from a comprehensive and internally consistent theological framework developed and refined over two millennia of rigorous intellectual tradition—from Augustine and Aquinas to the Reformed scholastics and beyond.

The natural law tradition, articulated most fully within Christian philosophy, holds that moral truths are not human inventions but features of reality, grounded in the nature and will of God and accessible through reason illuminated by revelation. Law, on this view, is not merely the command of the sovereign or the preference of the majority; it is an ordinance of reason directed toward the common good, promulgated by one who has care of the community—ultimately, under God. A Christian commonwealth would simply make explicit what any coherent legal order implicitly requires: a transcendent standard by which human laws are measured and found adequate or wanting.

Without such a standard, legal positivism—the view that law is whatever the state declares it to be—becomes the default philosophy. And legal positivism provides no principled basis for resisting tyranny. If law is merely power, then the only check on state authority is competing power. The Christian tradition, by contrast, insists that the state itself stands under judgment, that rulers are accountable to a law they did not write and cannot amend. Far from enabling tyranny, a Christian constitutional order would be the most robust possible bulwark against it.

II. The Historical Argument: Christianity and the Foundations of the American Order

The claim that the United States was founded as a secular state is, at best, an oversimplification and, at worst, a historical distortion. The First Amendment's prohibition on the establishment of religion was originally understood as preventing the federal government from privileging one Christian denomination over others or interfering with the established churches that several states maintained well into the nineteenth century. It was a federalism provision, not a secularism provision. The idea that it mandated a religion-free public square would have been incomprehensible to its authors.

The broader intellectual and cultural context of the founding was overwhelmingly Christian. The Declaration of Independence grounds its entire argument in theological claims: that human beings are "created" equal, that they are "endowed by their Creator" with certain unalienable rights, and that the moral law to which the colonies appealed was the law of "Nature's God." These are not rhetorical flourishes; they are the foundational premises of the American political argument. Remove them, and the Declaration's logic collapses.

The colonial and early state constitutions are even more explicit. The Massachusetts Constitution of 1780, drafted primarily by John Adams, declared it the duty of the legislature to require "the institution of the public worship of God and the support and maintenance of public Protestant teachers of piety, religion, and morality." Multiple state constitutions required officeholders to profess Christian faith. The Northwest Ordinance of 1787, passed by the same Congress that drafted the First Amendment, declared that "religion, morality, and knowledge, being necessary to good government and the happiness of mankind, schools and other means of education shall forever be encouraged."

Even those founders most sympathetic to Enlightenment rationalism—Jefferson and Franklin—operated within a broadly Christian moral universe and recognized the indispensability of religious conviction to republican government. Washington's Farewell Address went further, arguing that "of all the dispositions and habits which lead to political prosperity, religion and morality are indispensable supports" and questioning whether morality could be maintained "in exclusion of religious principle."

The historical argument is not that the founders established a theocracy—they did not—but that they operated within a Christian moral and intellectual framework that they regarded as essential to the republic's survival. The progressive secularization of American governance represents not fidelity to the founding vision but a departure from it. To reconstitute the United States as an explicitly Christian commonwealth would not be an innovation; it would be, in important respects, a restoration.

III. The Failure of Secular Liberalism

The strongest argument for Christian governance may be the mounting evidence that secular liberalism, whatever its historical accomplishments, is failing on its own terms.

The Crisis of Meaning. Secular societies are experiencing an epidemic of despair. Depression, anxiety, suicide, and substance abuse have risen sharply across the Western world, particularly among young people. Deaths of despair—from drugs, alcohol, and suicide—now claim more American lives annually than car accidents. The sociological literature increasingly identifies a "meaning crisis" at the root of this suffering: a pervasive sense that life has no ultimate purpose, that individual existence is cosmically insignificant, that moral commitments are arbitrary preferences rather than responses to reality.

Christianity addresses this crisis at its source. It offers a comprehensive account of human purpose: that human beings are created for communion with God and with one another, that suffering has redemptive meaning, that individual lives participate in an eternal narrative, that moral striving is not futile but directed toward a real and attainable good. No secular philosophy has proven capable of providing a substitute of comparable depth and resilience.

The Dissolution of the Family. The family is the foundational unit of every civilization, and it is disintegrating under secular governance. Rates of divorce, out-of-wedlock birth, cohabitation, and voluntary childlessness have risen dramatically. The consequences are well-documented and devastating: children raised without married parents are significantly more likely to experience poverty, abuse, educational failure, criminal involvement, and psychological distress. The secular state has proven unable to arrest this trend because it has no coherent account of why marriage and family deserve privileged status—having reduced marriage from a sacred covenant to a contractual arrangement terminable at will.

Christian governance would restore the family to its proper place in the social order. Christian theology provides a robust account of marriage as a permanent, conjugal union ordered toward mutual sanctification and the procreation and education of children. Law shaped by these principles would discourage divorce, incentivize marriage and childbearing, and structure social institutions around the family rather than the autonomous individual.

Moral Incoherence. Secular liberalism is increasingly unable to adjudicate its own moral conflicts. It simultaneously asserts that all cultures are equal and that cultures practicing female genital mutilation or honor killing are wrong. It insists on absolute individual autonomy while demanding expansive state intervention. It proclaims the supreme value of tolerance while enforcing rigid ideological conformity in institutions from universities to corporations. It champions "human rights" while providing no coherent philosophical account of what a human right is or where it comes from.

This incoherence is not accidental; it is structural. A political order that refuses to acknowledge any transcendent moral authority has no resources for resolving deep moral disagreements except power. The result is not the reasoned discourse that liberal theorists imagine but an increasingly bitter culture war in which competing groups struggle to capture the state and impose their preferences on others. The "neutral" public square has become a battleground precisely because it is not and cannot be neutral.

A Christian commonwealth would not eliminate moral disagreement, but it would provide a shared framework within which disagreement can be intelligently conducted. When citizens and legislators share a common understanding of human nature, moral law, and the purpose of government, deliberation becomes possible. When they share nothing, politics degenerates into mere faction.

The Expansion of State Power. One of the central ironies of secular liberalism is that the retreat of religious authority has been accompanied not by greater freedom but by the relentless expansion of state power. As mediating institutions—churches, families, local communities, voluntary associations—have weakened, the state has moved to fill the vacuum. The result is a society in which the individual stands increasingly alone before an omnipresent bureaucratic apparatus that regulates everything from speech to child-rearing to the acceptable range of opinion.

Christianity provides the most potent intellectual and institutional counterweight to state absolutism. The Christian tradition insists on the reality of spheres of authority that the state did not create and may not absorb: the family, the church, and the individual conscience bound to God. The doctrine of sphere sovereignty, articulated in the Reformed tradition, and the principle of subsidiarity, developed in Catholic social teaching, both hold that the state must respect the integrity and autonomy of these prior institutions. A Christian constitutional order would limit state power not merely through procedural mechanisms (checks and balances, bills of rights) but through substantive recognition that the state is not the highest authority and may not claim the total allegiance of its citizens.

IV. Addressing Objections

The case against Christian theocracy is familiar and must be met directly.

"Theocracy leads to tyranny." This is the most common objection and the least historically informed. Christianity has been associated with every form of government from monarchy to democracy, and the relationship between Christian governance and political liberty is far more complex than the caricature suggests. It was Christian principles that generated the concepts of constitutionalism, limited government, the rule of law, and the inherent rights of persons. The Magna Carta was produced by Christian bishops and barons appealing to Christian principles. The abolition of slavery was driven overwhelmingly by Christian conviction. The civil rights movement was led from Christian pulpits.

Moreover, the argument proves too much. Every ideology, including secular liberalism, has been associated with oppression. The explicitly secular regimes of the twentieth century—the Soviet Union, Maoist China, revolutionary France—produced atrocities on a scale that dwarfs anything attributable to Christian governance. If the capacity for abuse disqualifies a governing philosophy, secularism is disqualified far more decisively than Christianity.

The relevant question is not whether any system can be abused—all can—but which system contains the most robust internal resources for self-correction. Christianity, with its doctrines of original sin (which engenders suspicion of concentrated power), divine judgment (which holds rulers accountable), and the supreme authority of God over the state (which delegitimizes tyranny), is better equipped to restrain government than any secular alternative.

"What about religious minorities?" A Christian commonwealth need not be oppressive toward non-Christians. The Christian tradition itself provides resources for generous treatment of religious minorities. The parable of the wheat and the tares counsels patience; the Golden Rule demands respect; the dignity of every person as an image-bearer of God requires that even those in error be treated with justice and compassion. Historical Christian polities have often extended significant protections to minority communities—medieval Christendom's treatment of Jewish communities, while imperfect, was frequently more tolerant than contemporary secular treatments of dissenters.

The honest response, however, is that a Christian commonwealth would indeed privilege Christianity in its public life, its legal reasoning, and its educational institutions. This is not oppression; it is simply the coherent expression of the community's deepest convictions. Every political order privileges some values and marginalizes others. Secular liberalism privileges individual autonomy, expressive freedom, and materialist assumptions—and marginalizes traditional religious conviction with increasing aggressiveness. The question is not whether a society will have a dominant moral framework but whether that framework will be true.

"You can't legislate morality." This objection rests on a confusion. All legislation is the legislation of morality. Every law embodies a moral judgment: that theft is wrong, that contracts should be honored, that children should not be exploited. The question is never whether morality will be legislated but whose morality will prevail. The claim that morality should not be legislated is itself a moral claim—and one that, taken seriously, would make all law impossible.

"Which Christianity?" This is a practical challenge, not a principled objection. Christians disagree on many doctrinal matters, but there is a broad consensus on fundamental moral and political principles across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions: the dignity of the human person, the sanctity of life, the centrality of the family, the reality of natural law, the obligation of justice, the limits of state authority. A Christian constitutional order could be built on this shared foundation while accommodating denominational diversity in matters of worship and ecclesiology—much as the early American states maintained Christian establishments while differing in denominational affiliation.

V. A Vision of Christian Governance

What would a Christian commonwealth look like in practice? Not a caricature of theocratic tyranny, but a political order constituted on the following principles:

  1. Constitutional acknowledgment of God's sovereignty. The fundamental law would recognize that political authority is delegated by God and accountable to divine law. This is not unprecedented; numerous national constitutions contain similar provisions.

  2. Natural law as the basis of legislation. Laws would be measured against the natural moral law as understood in the Christian intellectual tradition. This would not require legislators to cite Scripture in debate (though they could), but to reason from a shared understanding of human nature and the common good.

  3. Protection of life from conception to natural death. A consistent ethic of life, rooted in the Christian conviction that every human being is created in God's image, would inform law and policy on issues from abortion to euthanasia to capital punishment.

  4. Support for the family as the foundational social institution. Marriage law, tax policy, education policy, and social services would be ordered toward strengthening the married, two-parent family. Divorce would be discouraged through legal and cultural means. The right and responsibility of parents to educate and form their children would be vigorously protected.

  5. Economic justice grounded in Christian social teaching. Both the acquisitive individualism of unfettered capitalism and the totalizing control of socialism would be rejected in favor of an economic order informed by the principles of subsidiarity, solidarity, and distributive justice. Property rights would be respected but understood as stewardship. The needs of the poor would be a central concern of public policy.

  6. Institutional pluralism and subsidiarity. The state would respect the autonomy of churches, families, schools, and voluntary associations. Government would intervene only when lower-order institutions fail to fulfill their functions and would always prefer the most local solution.

  7. Freedom of conscience within a Christian framework. Non-Christians would retain civil rights and the freedom to worship according to their consciences. Public institutions, however, would reflect Christian convictions, and the law would be shaped by Christian moral reasoning.

  8. Education in virtue. Public education would aim not merely at economic productivity but at the formation of virtuous citizens. This would include instruction in Christian moral philosophy, the Western intellectual tradition, and the obligations of citizenship.

VI. Conclusion

The proposal advanced here will strike many as radical, reactionary, or dangerous. But it is, in truth, none of these. It is radical only in the sense of returning to roots—to the philosophical and theological convictions that built Western civilization and animated the American founding. It is reactionary only if one accepts the dubious premise that every historical change constitutes progress. And it is dangerous only if one believes that a civilization can sustain itself indefinitely on moral capital it refuses to replenish.

The secular experiment has been tried. Its fruits are before us: a society of unprecedented material abundance and unprecedented spiritual poverty, of expansive individual freedom and pervasive loneliness, of proclaimed tolerance and escalating mutual hostility. The experiment has not failed entirely—it has preserved and extended certain genuine goods—but it has reached the limits of its internal resources. It cannot answer the questions that matter most: Why are we here? What do we owe each other? What is the good life? On what authority?

Christianity can answer these questions. It has answered them for two thousand years, across every culture and circumstance, with intellectual depth, moral seriousness, and pastoral compassion. It built the universities, the hospitals, the legal systems, and the moral intuitions that secular liberalism now claims as its own achievements. It can build again.

The question before us is not whether America will be guided by ultimate commitments—it will be, as every society must be. The question is whether those commitments will be acknowledged honestly and grounded coherently, or whether we will continue the increasingly desperate pretense that a civilization can live without a soul. A Christian commonwealth offers not theocratic oppression but the restoration of coherence—a political order that knows what it believes, why it believes it, and to whom it is ultimately accountable.

The God who endowed us with unalienable rights did not intend to be acknowledged only in the breach. It is time to welcome Him back into the public square—not as a guest, but as the sovereign He has always been.
